sentences.text: The genus Zhuchengtitan contains only one species, Z. zangjiazhuangensis, known from a single humerus discovered near Zhucheng, Shandong, China.
Specimen ZJZ-57 is mostly complete but has suffered significant damage to the outer edges of the top and bottom ends and the deltopectoral crest.
The top end of the humerus is 0.55 times the length of the entire bone, a proportion extreme compared to other titanosaurs because the inner edge angles more sharply inwards there than at the bottom.
A prominent deltopectoral crest extends down to the midshaft and sideways to occupy the outer width of the bone, bearing a hook-like process extending about halfway down its length.
Researchers uncovered the humerus and other sauropod bones at the Zangjiazhuang Quarry in 2008.
The species was formally described in 2017 by Mo Jinyou, Wang Kebai, Chen Shuqing, Wang Peiye, and Xu Xing.
The genus name Zhuchengtitan combines the location Zhucheng with the Greek suffix titan.
Thousands of Shantungosaurus fossils found at the site likely represent victims of a sudden mass mortality event.
Mo and colleagues assigned Zhuchengtitan to the family Saltasauridae based on specific humeral traits.
Researchers hypothesized that Zhuchengtitan may be closely related to Opisthocoelicaudia, but noted this needs confirmation from additional fossils.

Dating of a basalt layer places the Hongtuya Member at 73.5 million years old, corresponding to the Campanian age of the Cretaceous, while Zhuchengtitan lived approximately 72 million years ago during the Maastrichtian.
